$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)+\overset{f(t)}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}},\,Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & -2{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)$ and the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t)$ of the system.
${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)=\,\,$ $2{e}^{t}$ $\,,\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=\,\,$ $\frac{2}{3}$
{{field-1}} {{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & -2{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}\cdot 2{e}^{3t}-(-2{e}^{3t})\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3t} & 2{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2t}}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3t} & 2{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} \\ -2{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 2{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -2{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} \\ \frac{2}{3}{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & -2{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2{e}^{t} \\ \frac{2}{3}{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-2}} by substitution.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-4}} into $\text{L1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ Let's substitute ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$ from $\text{L4}$ into $\text{L3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+\cancel{AΦu(t)}=\cancel{AΦu(t)}+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3}\text{ and }\text{L4}$ by substitution.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$

questions.problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 \\ 9 & -8\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}5t \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form
$x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}-\,\,\frac{1}{4}$ {{field-1}} .
$90t+45$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}5t \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot 3{e}^{-2t}}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5t \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-5t{e}^{2t} \\ 15t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 15t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-5t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-5\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -5t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-5t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-5\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{2}\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=15t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=15\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 15t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =15t\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot 15\,\text{d}t \\  & =-15t{e}^{-t}+\int 15{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-15t{e}^{-t}-15{e}^{-t} \\  & =-15{e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\ -15{e}^{-t}(t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}10(1-2t)-60(t+1) \\ 15(1-2t)-60(t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}80t+50 \\ 90t+45\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}t \\ 3t\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form
$x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+\,\,\frac{1}{2}$ {{field-1}} .
$6t-6$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}t \\ 3t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}t \\ 3t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2t{e}^{2t} \\ 3t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-2t{e}^{2t} \\ 3t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-2t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-2\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-2\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-t{e}^{2t}+\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t{e}^{2t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=3\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(3t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =3t{e}^{t}-3{e}^{t} \\  & =3{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\ 3{e}^{t}(t-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}(1-2t)+6(t-1) \\ 6(t-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}4t-5 \\ 6t-6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

fields.input_html: 4t−5
